chapter: Other bands, mutes, arrangers and composers
title: Mutes and the cup mute he invented in 1917
summary: DeDroit describes fiber straight mutes and how he made a cup mute from a Salisbury cigarette can in 1917 without copyrighting it.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Well, you mentioned the mutes. When did mutes become, what kind of mutes were really popular? Straight mutes. Straight mutes?

Yeah. There was a, Mr. Peterson who was the dean of all the drummers, he taught all the drummers, his name was George Peterson, he used to make them out of fiber. Out of what? Fiber, some kind of fiber. Red. Fiber? Oh, I call it fiber. It's a stiff material. It's a cardboard. And I invented a lot of mutes but I failed to have them copyrighted. But the Dixie Music Company in Chicago had them copyrighted. I invented the cup mute. I used to have a large Salisbury can attached to a straight mute. And when I played it, it was a cup mute.
A large Salisbury cigarette can. It was large, I say large Salisbury because that was the one I used. There might have been other.
How did you get the idea? Just having it occur to you?
I used to play through the big end of a megaphone, through the small end of a megaphone, through a tin can with a rubber plunger, anything for weird effects. A different effect.
And what year would that have been that you?

I did that when, well that's when I started with my success, in 1917. 1917, you got the cup mute then. I took a large Salisbury can and I got some kind of something, put a hole in it, clamped it onto the straight mute and I fixed it in the right direction so I could get a little tone and all of a sudden I had a nice tone, had a nice cup mute. So it was. If I had to have that copyright, I'd have been rich because they came out in different sizes and different levels.
You wouldn't have had to play all these years.
